candidats.resume: Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 doesn't generate images the way other AI models do. Instead of computing pixels, the language model writes Python code that places hundreds of thousands of simulated brushstrokes on a virtual canvas, complete with bristle texture and paint application. A single photorealistic parking garage scene took roughly 700,000 strokes, according to Anthropic employee Jake Eaton. candidats.resume: Megaspeed, the firm owned by ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's former lover Alice Huang, arranged nearly $12 billion in Nvidia chip orders for Chinese companies between 2024 and 2025, according to the WSJ. candidats.titre: Australia's central bank finds AI hitting young workers first, especially in software and customer service
candidats.resume: Australia's central bank sees early signs that AI is hitting young entry-level workers in highly exposed jobs like software development and customer service. Since ChatGPT launched, job postings and employment among 15- to 24-year-olds in those fields have dropped more sharply than among older workers. Author Mike Major cautions against jumping to conclusions, however, noting that business cycle shifts and remote work trends could also explain the numbers. candidats.titre: Feux d’artifice : quelques minutes de fête, des coûts durables pour la santé et l’environnement
candidats.resume: Pollution de l’air, blessures, stress des animaux et coûts de santé… une partie de la facture des feux d’artifices est supportée par la collectivité. Rawpixel.com/Shutterstock (no reuse) L’ESSENTIEL Le plaisir des feux d’artifice ne dure que quelques minutes, mais une partie de leur coût retombe sur des gens qui ne les ont ni achetés ni admirés : c’est ce que les économistes appellent une « externalité négative ». La facture se lit d’abord à l’hôpital, avec 123 admissions en Angleterre en 2024-2025 en lien avec les feux d’artifice, et jusque dans le ciel, où les oiseaux s’envolent en masse pendant les tirs. En Grande-Bretagne, une consultation publique, proposant de limiter leur niveau sonore, vient de s’achever. Au-delà du débat sur leur interdiction, mieux vaut chercher d’autres façons de faire la fête qui procurent autant de joie, mais occasionnent moins de dégâts. Chaque année, au Royaume-Uni, pour Bonfire Night, la nuit des feux de joie (célébrée le 5 novembre, en souvenir de l’échec de la conspiration des Poudres, un projet d’attentat contre le Parlement en 1605), des particuliers achètent une boîte de feux d’artifice pour offrir un spectacle coloré à leurs proches. En quelques minutes, tout est fini. Mais le prix sur la boîte ne reflète pas tous les coûts cachés : la fumée inhalée par les voisins par exemple, les animaux qui en ressortent perturbés ou encore les services publics mobilisés quand les choses tournent mal… La question n’est pas de savoir si les fêtes avec des feux d’artifice sont agréables, mais si ceux qui en profitent ont conscience de leur coût…

candidats.titre: Le pastoralisme, risque ou solution face au changement climatique ? L’évolution du regard porté par les COP climat
candidats.resume: Plusieurs centaines de millions de personnes dans le monde vivent du pastoralisme. Il peut être source d’inspiration pour penser et pour accompagner les autres formes d’agriculture, le changement agraire ou encore notre perception de la nature. L’ouvrage Penser avec le pastoralisme. Itinéraires de recherche (librement téléchargeable en ebook), récemment publié aux éditions Quae (coordination Véronique Ancey, Serena Ferrari et Claire Aubron), explore ces enjeux. À l’occasion de la COP31 sur le climat, qui se tient en Turquie du 9 au 20 novembre, nous reproduisons une partie du chapitre consacré à la place du pastoralisme pour les experts du Groupe d'experts intergouvernemental sur l'évolution du climat (Giec), les COP climat et la diplomatie mondiale. Bien que la contribution de l’élevage au changement climatique soit désormais largement reconnue, ce secteur est longtemps resté en marge de l’agenda climatique international dans le cadre du Giec et n’y a été intégré que tardivement. Si l’agriculture a commencé à être prise en compte à la fin des années 2000, l’élevage n’a véritablement émergé dans les discussions qu’à partir de 2011. L’analyse des contributions déterminées au niveau national (rapport « NDC ») ( dont les États doivent régulièrement relever l’ambition dans le cadre de l’accord de Paris , ndlr ) met clairement en évidence cette marginalisation persistante dans l’action climatique. Au 30 septembre 2022, parmi les 164 pays ayant soumis une NDC, seuls 54 % mentionnaient explicitement l’élevage. Parmi eux, 59 pays intégraient le bétail dans leurs engagements…

candidats.titre: « Si je te punis, c’est pour ton bien », vraiment ? Contre l’adultisme, penser une éducation mutuelle
candidats.resume: L’ESSENTIEL Les réflexions sur l’adultisme montrent que de bonnes intentions éducatives peuvent masquer des rapports de forces. Nous avons été formés à voir dans l’âge une supériorité. Mais l’argument de l’expérience n’est-il pas la voie de l’arbitraire ? Pour être émancipatrice, l’éducation ne peut se fonder sur l’infantilisation et suppose d’apprendre à dire non. Parce que je suis plus ancienne ou ancien que toi, ai-je le droit de te donner des ordres, même si tu ne le veux pas, en estimant que « c’est pour ton bien » ? Ai-je le droit de t’empêcher de faire ce que tu désires, en jugeant que « ça te protège » ? Être adulte, ce serait ainsi croire dans le blanc-seing des bonnes intentions éducatives. Nous avons toutes et tous été éduqués à croire que la prise d’âge donne des droits sur celles et ceux qui ont moins vécu . Comme si l’expérience de vie était un butin qu’on détient par capitalisation. Or, en éducation, nous savons que les expériences sont qualitativement formatrices, ce n’est pas leur quantité qui compte. Une vie routinière, conformiste, des traumas qui mènent à la compulsion de répétition ou à des addictions, malgré des expériences maintes fois réitérées, ne font pas de nous des personnes fiables ou légitimes à imposer nos vues aux autres. Il n’y a donc aucune raison d’être dupe des pseudo-justifications des anciennes et des anciens : « Tu n’as pas assez d’expérience » ; « Tu verras quand tu seras grand·e »… Mais alors, pourquoi la posture sociale d’éducateur ou d’éducatrice (qu’on soit parent, dans les métiers de l’animation ou de l’enseignement)…

candidats.titre: COP31 : la Bourse ne récompense plus la découverte de réserves d’hydrocarbures en cas d’exposition aux risques réglementaires environnementaux
candidats.resume: L’ESSENTIEL Près de 60 % des réserves mondiales de pétrole et de gaz fossile devraient rester dans le sol d’ici à 2050 pour tenir l’objectif de contenir la hausse de température moyenne de la planète à 1,5 °C. Une étude, portant sur 16 majors pétrolières, souligne que leurs réserves pèsent sur leurs performances boursières lorsque la réglementation se durcit. Ces investissements dans les hydrocarbures deviennent non viables, des actifs dits « échoués ». Malgré la transition vers une économie bas carbone et la COP31 , qui se tient en Turquie jusqu’au 20 novembre, l’industrie du pétrole et du gaz continue d’attirer d’importants appétits des investisseurs. En 2026, les investissements mondiaux dans le pétrole devraient s’établir à un peu moins de 500 milliards de dollars états-uniens tandis que ceux consacrés au gaz devraient s’établir à près de 330 milliards de dollars (298,6 milliards d’euros). Cette situation soulève un paradoxe. Alors que la transition énergétique vise à réduire la dépendance aux énergies fossiles, les entreprises continuent de découvrir et de développer de nouvelles réserves d’hydrocarbure. Une question se pose alors : ces réserves conserveront-elles la même valeur si de futures réglementations climatiques limitent leur exploitation ? Pour répondre à cette question, dans notre étude , nous avons analysé conjointement les réserves, l’exposition au risque réglementaire lié au changement climatique et les performances boursières de seize grandes entreprises pétrolières et gazières internationales – dont TotalEnergies, British Petroleum, Eni ou Petrobras –…

candidats.titre: Est-il encore possible de stabiliser la dette publique française ?
candidats.resume: L’ESSENTIEL La dette publique a une dynamique propre. Sa croissance et sa « soutenabilité » dépendent du taux de croissance et du taux d’inflation. L’efficacité d’une réduction des déficits publics dépend du choix de l’instrument budgétaire utilisé et du rythme de l’effort. Certaines mesures, en pesant sur la croissance du PIB, ont un impact négatif sur le taux d’endettement. La hausse des taux d’intérêt augmente la part du budget consacré au remboursement des intérêts. Une dette élevée accroît ces taux d’intérêt sur les marchés. L’adoption d’une règle budgétaire permettrait de réduire ces contraintes. À 3 595 milliards d’euros, soit 119 % du produit intérieur brut ( PIB ), la dette publique atteint un niveau record. a4.texte:
Meituan releases a 1.6-trillion-parameter agent model that never touched an Nvidia GPU
Meituan releases the weights for LongCat-2.5, a 1.6-trillion-parameter model built for AI agents. It was trained entirely on Chinese hardware and performs at the level US models like Claude Opus 5 reached a few months ago on coding benchmarks.
The LongCat team at Chinese food delivery company Meituan has released the weights for LongCat-2.5, one week after the model's official unveiling. LongCat-2.5 is built for agents that work through long, multi-step tasks autonomously, particularly coding. According to Meituan, it comes close to top Western models on several benchmarks.
LongCat-2.5 is a mixture-of-experts model that activates only a subset of its specialized subnetworks for each token it processes. Out of 1.6 trillion total parameters, roughly 48 billion are active per token. Through the API, the model handles up to one million tokens at once and generates responses up to 128,000 tokens long. It understands text, images, and video, responds in text, and lets users toggle reasoning on and off.
LongCat-2.5 converts images into tokens
LongCat-2.5 builds on its predecessor LongCat-2.0 and adds image understanding. Many multimodal models bolt on a separate image encoder after the fact. LongCat-2.5 instead converts images into tokens that the model processes alongside text, as is standard practice for today's LLMs. The approach draws on the research model LongCat-Next and aims to improve visual coding, design, and 3D tasks.
For reinforcement learning, the team used real software tasks from GitHub pull requests along with recreated agent failures. To make sure the model actually solved the tasks during training, the developers blocked internet access in the training environments, removed Git history and cached files, and had a language model check its solutions for tricks. The team also distilled the capabilities of several specialized teacher models for agent work, reasoning, and dialog into LongCat-2.5.
A sample deployment runs on 194 Huawei chips
Meituan quantizes the experts' weights and activations to 4-bit precision, which Chinese chips can process natively. In Meituan's load tests, throughput rises 43.3 percent for prompt processing and 42.77 percent for response generation compared with an 8-bit version. Meituan says accuracy stays on par with the uncompressed model.
This version is available in a separate repository. The self-hosting guide describes a cluster of 194 Huawei Ascend accelerators from the Atlas A2 series. Two handle image processing, 64 handle prompt ingestion, and 128 handle response generation. There's no guidance for Nvidia GPUs.
LongCat-2.5 trails Opus 5 slightly on terminal tasks
The LongCat team reports 88.4 points on Terminal Bench v2.1, a benchmark that measures how well agents solve command-line tasks. Meituan lists Claude Opus 5 at 89.1, GPT-5.6 Sol at 88.8, and Deepseek-V4.1-Flash at the top of the table with 90.6.
DeepSWE tests how well models fix bugs in real code repositories. Here LongCat-2.5 jumps from 9.7 to 64.6 points, placing it behind every other model in the table except Claude Opus 4.8, with Deepseek-V4.1-Flash leading at 74.2 and GPT-5.6 Sol at 72.7. The more recent Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol are not included in the table.
Terminal Bench v4.0, the harder variant, puts LongCat-2.5 at 38.5 points, slightly above GPT-5.6 Sol's 37.3 but well below Opus 5's 53.9. The model posts 91.9 on the web search benchmark BrowseComp, the highest score in the table, though Meituan ran this test in its own environment.
The weights are available under the MIT license, which allows commercial use, modification, and redistribution. Users can also try LongCat-2.5 in a chat interface at https://longcat.ai/. Its API supports both the OpenAI and Anthropic formats and plugs into agent harnesses like Claude Code, Codex, and Hermes. At launch, Meituan is charging a limited-time promotional price equivalent to roughly €0.27 per million input tokens and €1.07 per million output tokens.
Meituan says it trained the predecessor LongCat-2.0 in late June entirely on a cluster of more than 50,000 Chinese AI chips. Before that, the model ran anonymously as "Owl Alpha" on OpenRouter. Chinese open-weight models like Kimi K3.1 and GLM-5.3 have largely caught up with top US models on common benchmarks.
Open-weight models optimized for Chinese chips from the start make that hardware more attractive outside China too. Beyond multimodal agent models, Meituan is also working on image generators. The company previously released LongCat-Image, an open-source text-to-image model that gets by with just 6 billion parameters and prioritizes efficiency over sheer model size.

Australia's central bank finds AI hitting young workers first, especially in software and customer service
AI has barely displaced any jobs in Australia so far, but young workers entering highly exposed fields like software development are faring worse.
An analysis by Mike Major for Australia's central bank (RBA) built a monitoring system that focuses on the areas where effects are likely to appear first, namely entry-level workers and highly AI-exposed occupations such as programming, clerical work, and customer service.
According to the analysis, job postings have fallen across all groups since ChatGPT launched in late 2022, with the steepest drop in the highest-exposure group. In that group, workers aged 15 to 24 and young college graduates have weaker employment rates and higher unemployment than older workers.
Major cautions against drawing early conclusions, since the study does not establish direct causation and measures only theoretical exposure, not actual use by companies. Post-pandemic shifts in the business cycle or in remote work could also be driving the numbers. According to SEEK data, AI is complementing existing work while also creating new demand for AI skills.
Other studies paint a similar picture, with caveats
An August 2025 Stanford study based on millions of US payroll records found a similar pattern, with employment among 22- to 25-year-olds in AI-exposed occupations down 13 percent in relative terms since late 2022 and nearly 20 percent among young software developers. More experienced workers in the same occupations held steady or gained ground.
A March 2026 Anthropic study also found signs of declining hiring among 22- to 25-year-olds in exposed occupations, with job-finding rates down about 14 percent. It found no systematic rise in overall unemployment, however. Theoretical automation potential and actual AI use are far apart, according to the study.
Anthropic offers a company-level example. According to an internal review, the share of junior hires in technical roles has fallen from 27 percent to 9 percent since early 2025. In August 2026, AI agents across the company were already logging six times as many hours as human employees. Anthropic concedes that, as an extremely AI-intensive software company, it is a special case. Even so, researchers warn of a "tragedy of the cognitive commons", in which disappearing junior roles lead to a future shortage of experienced professionals, assuming those professionals are still needed.
A large study of 25,000 workers in Denmark confirms the lack of economy-wide impact. Despite a 64 percent AI adoption rate, researchers found no measurable changes in wages or hours worked. Workers saved an average of just 2.8 percent of their working time.
A January 2026 analysis of 10.6 million LinkedIn profiles and US unemployment data, however, cautions against blaming the downturn on AI alone. The research team led by Morgan Frank at the University of Pittsburgh found that the problems in exposed occupations started in early 2022, months before ChatGPT launched. Macroeconomic factors like the Fed's shift in interest rate policy or a correction after pandemic-era hiring surges may play a bigger role than previously assumed.
At the same time, AI is creating new demand. According to the World Economic Forum's "Future of Jobs Report 2025", 77 percent of surveyed companies are prioritizing upskilling over job cuts. WEF researchers project a net gain of 78 million jobs by 2030. According to LinkedIn, AI-related job postings grew sixfold in one year.

SOURCE 1 (The Decoder) :
OpenAI reassigns robotics researchers to other teams as general-purpose models might make specialized robotics AI unnecessary
Update –
The opening sentence of this article originally stated that OpenAI was "apparently disbanding its robotics team again." OpenAI has since clarified that it reorganized the team to work more closely with research and product and that robotics work continues. The opening sentence has been updated to reflect this.
OpenAI has reorganized its robotics team, though for different reasons than when it first disbanded the unit in 2020.
Rather than abandoning robotics, the company wants to accelerate it by folding researchers into other teams. Robotics researchers are moving to the main research team under Chief Research Officer Mark Chen, while the applied robotics and hardware teams join Greg Brockman's Applied organization.
OpenAI made the decision on such short notice that it had already booked a booth at the Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) in Austin, which then sat empty, Fortune reports. OpenAI apparently believes that general-purpose models like GPT-6 Astra can control robots directly, reducing the need for specialized robotics models.
In an Nvidia study, an Astra-powered agent achieved a 74.8 percent success rate on simulated robotics tasks, compared to 51 percent for the best specialized models. The tests used a simulated DROID robot, not a physical one.
A new robotics benchmark called StationeryBench compared GPT-6 Astra with Ai2's MolmoAct2 on five tasks involving desk objects on dual-arm YAM robotic arms. Across 200 trials, Astra fully completed 7 out of 100 tasks, while MolmoAct2 didn't complete a single one. Astra's average progress score was 46, compared to 12 for MolmoAct2. In another test, Astra running on a humanoid robot navigated and cleaned up a kitchen.
It remains unclear how much robotics data OpenAI and others incorporated during training. Other large general-purpose models from Anthropic and Google have also made recent progress on robotics tasks. Specialized robotics models may still have advantages in cost and reliability as well as speed and energy consumption, even if they don't generalize as well.

OpenAI had a robotics team in its early days but wound it down in 2020, with cofounder Wojciech Zaremba later citing limited robot data and a more efficient path toward artificial general intelligence (AGI)—the human-like AI that has been OpenAI’s goal since its founding—through other methods. The reorganization reflects a bet that is gaining traction across the AI industry: that general-purpose models built for language, code, and vision can also be used for “embodied AI”—where AI models control devices that can act in the physical world, such as robots, driverless cars, or drones. This would obviate the need to have separate robotics teams building specialized AI models just to be the digital “brains” for robots.

OpenAI seemed to confirm this view in its response to Fortune. It said that at the start of the year, the company’s researchers assumed the best way to make progress on robotics was to build on its work on AI models such as Sora, a video generation model that, in order to create realistic videos, had to have some implicit understanding of how the physical world works.

"Des courriers ont pu être lus" : ce que l'on sait de la cyberattaque contre Maileva, filiale de La Poste, qui a conduit au vol de données de 22 millions de personnes
La brigade de lutte contre la cybercriminalité a été chargée de l'enquête, a confirmé dimanche le parquet de Paris. Les investigations ont été ouvertes pour "atteinte à un système de traitement automatisé de données" par la section cybercriminalité du parquet parisien.
C'est l'une des cyberattaques les plus importantes commises en France. Maileva, une filiale du groupe La Poste, a annoncé samedi 14 novembre avoir été touchée par une cyberattaque de grande ampleur. Selon l'entreprise, les coordonnées de 22 millions de personnes ont été dérobées. Franceinfo vous explique ce que l'on sait de l'incident.
Une plateforme spécialisée dans l'envoi de courriers pour les entreprises
Maileva, plateforme française en ligne spécialisée dans l'envoi et la gestion de courriers et de documents professionnels, est une filiale de Docaposte, elle-même filiale du groupe La Poste. Elle revendique plus de 70 000 utilisateurs, et 180 millions de documents (bulletins de salaire, factures, recommandés…) envoyés en 2024, selon son site internet. Elle imprime et expédie des courriers pour de nombreuses grandes entreprises, mais aussi des institutions publiques, comme des bailleurs sociaux et des hôpitaux.
La Poste a annoncé samedi soir que Maileva avait été victime mi-septembre d'une cyberattaque de grande ampleur. L'entreprise n'a pas communiqué précisément sur la méthode d'intrusion des hackeurs. "C'est un scénario de cyberattaque classique, dans lequel les pirates ont attaqué un prestataire [Maileva] dans le but de récupérer des bases de données", souligne auprès de franceinfo Antoine Hautin, secrétaire général de l'entreprise de cybersécurité Almond.
Fin septembre, Docaposte avait suspendu les services de Maileva pendant six jours après une tentative de détournement de la plateforme, expliquait le 30 septembre le site spécialisé Solutions numériques et cybersécurités. L'entreprise avait alors fait état de "tentatives d'accès non autorisées à la plateforme", sans donner plus de détails.
Des noms et adresses postales ont fuité
La Poste a annoncé à l'AFP que les coordonnées de 22 millions de personnes avaient été collectées. Toutes sont des "destinataires des entreprises clientes de Maileva". Plusieurs bailleurs sociaux, comme Flandre Opale Habitat et Altéal ont signalé une fuite de données, liée à cette cyberattaque, début novembre. Les données exposées sont le prénom, le nom et l'adresse postale des personnes concernées. "Des informations administratives ou financières, comme un montant de facture", ont également été récupérées, précise Flandre Opale Habitat. "Cet incident pourrait avoir entraîné un accès non autorisé à des données personnelles contenues dans des courriers envoyés au cours des dix dernières années", ajoute le bailleur.
L'hôpital Foch de Suresnes, situé dans les Hauts-de-Seine, a aussi prévenu ses patients début novembre que "des courriers de relance de paiement" ont "pu être lus par un pirate informatique". "Ces courriers ne mentionnent ni la nature de vos soins, ni vos coordonnées bancaires", ajoute l'établissement, qui appelle à se méfier de "toute demande d'argent qui semblerait venir de l'hôpital".
La quantité de données volées est importante. "Maileva est un fournisseur qui présente un risque systémique, car il est utilisé par des dizaines de milliers d'organisations", rappelle Antoine Hautin. Les clients des entreprises concernées par la fuite de données doivent être prévenus par ces dernières, selon le règlement européen général sur la protection des données personnelles.
Un risque de réception de courriers frauduleux
L'un des risques principaux est l'envoi de courriers frauduleux aux personnes dont les coordonnées ont été dérobées. "Il faut faire attention aux courriers reçus qui peuvent ressembler à des lettres légitimes, car avec l'intelligence artificielle, on peut facilement automatiser les campagnes de fraude", souligne Antoine Hautin. En cas de "demande inhabituelle", le spécialiste conseille "de contacter l'émetteur par un autre canal".
Les données dérobées serviront à alimenter "des bases de données géantes sur le dark web", note Antoine Hautin. "Plus la fuite est récente, plus les informations sont fiables, il est donc possible d'alimenter en continu une sorte de fiche sur chaque citoyen, avec des informations précises comme vos liens avec un hôpital ou un bailleur social", détaille le vice-président d'Almond.
Une enquête en cours
Dans son communiqué, Maileva a précisé avoir notifié la Commission nationale de l'informatique et des libertés et déposé une plainte. "Conformément à la réglementation, toutes les entreprises concernées ont été informées de l'incident par Maileva", a ajouté l'entreprise.
La brigade de lutte contre la cybercriminalité a été chargée de l'enquête, a confirmé dimanche le parquet de Paris, sollicité par l'AFP. Les investigations ont été ouvertes pour "atteinte à un système de traitement automatisé de données" par la section cybercriminalité du parquet parisien.
Ce n'est pas la première fois que le groupe La Poste est touché par une cyberattaque d'ampleur. En décembre 2025, quelques jours avant Noël, l'entreprise avait été victime d'une cyberattaque massive, revendiquée par des hackeurs prorusses, contre ses services en ligne. L'accès à la Banque postale et aux services de suivi des colis avait été perturbé pendant plusieurs jours.
Au-delà de La Poste, les attaques informatiques se sont multipliées ces derniers mois contre des entreprises ou organismes publics. Début novembre, Crédit Mutuel Arkéa a déclaré avoir été la cible d'une cyberattaque d'un montant de l'ordre de 100 millions d'euros. France Travail avait fait l'objet d'une attaque massive début 2024, avec un risque de divulgation de données personnelles concernant 43 millions de personnes.
"On vit un moment de multiplication des cyberattaques" a rappelé le ministre des Comptes publics David Amiel sur franceinfo dimanche. "Pendant trop longtemps, les questions de cybersécurité ont été reléguées à l'arrière-plan", a-t-il regretté, appelant à des investissements sur ce sujet.

Quel que soit le résultat de l’élection présidentielle du printemps, tous les députés s’attendent à une dissolution de l’Assemblée nationale dans la foulée. Mais si des législatives étaient organisées en juin 2027, la carte électorale serait basée sur les données démographiques de l’année 2006. La France est l’un des rares pays où le redécoupage des circonscriptions n’est pas régulier et les deux réorganisations conduites par le passé ont laissé des traces. Depuis 1958, la carte électorale a d’abord été retouchée en 1986, sous l’égide de Charles Pasqua, ministre de l’intérieur. En 2009, cette mission a été menée à bien par Alain Marleix, secrétaire d’Etat aux collectivités territoriales, également spécialiste de la carte électorale au sein de l’Union pour un mouvement populaire (UMP).
Les socialistes avaient alors dénoncé un « tripatouillage électoral » de la droite. « Je ne garde pas de mauvais souvenirs de ce découpage, que j’avais trouvé plutôt républicain », nuance dix-sept ans plus tard Bruno Le Roux, à l’époque député et spécialiste de la question au Parti socialiste (PS). « Ce ne fut pas un charcutage total et ils n’ont pas contrevenu aux règles », concède Christophe Borgel, alors secrétaire national du PS aux élections, qui tempère tout de même : « A chaque fois qu’ils ont pu procéder en faveur de leurs intérêts, ils l’ont fait en regroupant des cantons de gauche pour que les autres circonscriptions soient plus difficiles pour nous. » Et de donner en exemple des cartes curieuses, comme celles de la Somme ou du Rhône.
En France, c’est le ministère de l’intérieur qui redessine la carte électorale. Quand s’ouvre un chantier de redécoupage, le ministre qui tient les ciseaux devient vite le membre du gouvernement le plus sollicité. « Il suffisait de voir le nombre de mots que recevait Alain Marleix pendant les séances de questions d’actualité », constate Bruno Le Roux. Le ministère est tenu au respect de plusieurs règles : les circonscriptions doivent être continues et respecter le cadre départemental, ce qui favorise les territoires ruraux. L’écart maximal de population doit être de 20 % par rapport à la moyenne départementale et les cantons inférieurs à 40 000 habitants ne peuvent être divisés. Pour le reste, il a les mains libres.

"La réponse que Les Restos du coeur apportent à la précarité en France est essentielle, mais elle atteint ses limites", affirme leur président, Jean-Michel Richard.
"La pauvreté atteint des niveaux inédits depuis des décennies" en France. He accused Qatar, which has hosted Hamas’s political office and funds Al Jazeera, of dominating that arena. “We completely gave that arena to Qatar, and they are shifting the narrative,” he said.
An Arab in the Israeli army
Haddad served in the Golani Brigade and was badly wounded by a Hezbollah anti-tank missile in the 2006 Lebanon war. “It was my Jewish brothers in arms who saved my life and who brought me back to Israel,” he said.
Arab citizens, about a fifth of Israel’s population, are exempt from compulsory service, and Haddad volunteered.
“I, as an Arab, was a commander over Jewish soldiers in the IDF,” he said, rejecting the charge that Israel is an apartheid state.
In 2024 he lit a torch at Israel’s official Independence Day ceremony. “This is something huge for an Israeli, yes, but for an Arab Israeli, it’s absolutely crazy,” he said.
Criticism of Arab-led parties
Arab-led parties won a record 19 seats in the October 27 election, and their backing helped opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot win the mandate to form a government. Haddad said the result showed Israel’s democracy works, but he accused the parties’ leaders of neglecting their own voters.
“When the election comes, all the leaders stop talking about Gaza, stop talking about Jenin and Ramallah, and finally they start talking again about Nazareth and Haifa,” he said. “They’re lying to us, time after time.”
He singled out Ahmad Tibi, the veteran head of Ta’al. “He tells you that Israel is an apartheid state. He tells you that he doesn’t want Israel as a Jewish state,”
He also said Tibi was protected by his parliamentary immunity. “He hit a cop, but because he’s a politician, he has immunity. No one can do anything to him,” Haddad said.
Haddad said he had once been kept out of a Knesset committee session chaired by Joint List lawmaker Aida Touma-Sliman on the claim that Israel is an apartheid state.
“I told her, ‘You guys are actually the apartheid, because you don’t want to listen to me, and I’m one of you, an Arab just like you,’” he said. “Pure apartheid toward me.”
He also cited Sami Abu Shehadeh, head of the Balad party, who withdrew from the election in October after the Central Elections Committee voted to bar him over remarks after the October 7 attack.
“They don’t want to set a precedent,” Haddad said of the Supreme Court, which recommended the withdrawal rather than ruling. “I’m all for freedom of speech, until you start to incite to terrorism.”
Teaching children to die
Haddad said the Guards’ proxies indoctrinate children from an early age, and that education can work in both directions. He praised the United Arab Emirates, which designated the Muslim Brotherhood a terrorist group in 2014 and later began teaching the Holocaust in schools.
Of children raised by Hamas in Gaza and Hezbollah in Lebanon, he said: “When you arrive at age 12, you’re already serving in their terrorist organization, completely brainwashed. When you arrive at age 16, you’re ready to die.”
Haddad said he hoped Israelis and Iranians would build a common front.
"Together, the people of Israel and the people of Iran, we can actually do it," he said.

SOURCE 1 (South China Morning Post) :
The state leaders of China, the United States and Russia will hold a trilateral meeting in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen on Thursday on the sidelines of the Apec leaders’ summit, Beijing said on Monday. The high-stakes meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping and his counterparts Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin will mark the first time the leaders of the world’s three foremost nuclear and geopolitical powers sit down together in a three-way format. The announcement follows...

SOURCE 2 (Al Jazeera) :
US President Donald Trump, China’s President Xi Jinping and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin will hold their first trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China’s Shenzhen, the White House has confirmed.
On Friday, Washington also confirmed Trump’s attendance at the summit, which will take place from November 18-19.
Talks will focus on nuclear proliferation, the White House said. But they come amid significant global turbulence: Russia’s war in Ukraine, the US-Israeli war on Iran and ongoing trade tensions between Washington and Beijing.
“I think what we’ll see is some pretty impressive photo-ops with a lot of really bombastic rhetoric from Trump,” Simon Mabon, a professor of international politics at the UK’s Lancaster University, told Al Jazeera. However, he added, the three “collectively or unilaterally, are not able to bring about an end to the conflict in Iran or Ukraine”.
So what does each side want and what will be the likely outcome?
Here’s what we know:
What’s on the agenda?
Each leader has his own priorities, but there are some issues all will want to discuss.
New nuclear treaty
A top issue for Russia and the US is the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START), which lapsed in February. The treaty was first signed in 2010 and caps US and Russian strategic nuclear arsenals.
Russia currently possesses the largest number of warheads, followed by the US and then China, which is rapidly building up its own arsenal.
Trump previously rejected Russia’s proposal to extend the treaty after it expired, demanding instead a “new, improved and modernised” deal that includes Beijing.
China is understood, however, to be reluctant to join an agreement it was not involved in forming.
A senior Trump administration official told Reuters this topic will start the conversation but that “we do not expect to get any kind of agreement”.
US-Israel war on Iran
Officials also say the world leaders will discuss the Iran war, which the US and Israel launched on February 28. While full-scale strikes have, for now, ceased, the conflict remains in a deadlock.
After more than 100 days, the critical Strait of Hormuz remains closed, and oil and gas prices are still volatile as ships in the strait continue to face Iranian strikes and seamines. One-third of China’s crude oil supply transited the strait before the war. The conflict is also hampering demand for Chinese exports.
Russia, meanwhile, has profited from rising energy prices and recent sanctions relief from Washington amid supply crunches – particularly of diesel.
China-US trade rivalry
Trade wars and the race to control microchips used to power artificial intelligence are straining relations between Beijing and Washington.
Trump hit China with a 145 percent tax hike last year, while Beijing retaliated by imposing 125 percent levies on US imports. Tensions mounted further over China’s restrictions on exports of rare earth minerals needed to manufacture advanced chips and other technology.
The two countries have since reduced tariffs and struck several deals following Trump and Xi’s meetings in South Korea and Washington However, the recent scandal at chip firm Nvidia has prompted the US to allege that China was spying on CEO Jensen Huang. Beijing denies this.
Will the Ukraine war be discussed?
It is very unlikely. A Trump administration official told reporters the US president will not bring up Russia’s war on Ukraine, although Kremlin officials previously suggested the conflict could be discussed.
China, an ally of Moscow’s, has said the Ukraine war is a European issue.
US officials also note that Washington is pursuing peace talks, with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visiting both Ukraine and Russia this week. “China is not really a part of that track, so it doesn’t seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there,” an official told reporters.
President Trump has accused Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of “not wanting” to end the war, while Kyiv has reiterated allegations that the US has restricted its Starlink satellite connection that allows it to operate attack drones. Trump has also blamed Ukraine for soaring diesel prices because of its strikes on Russian oil facilities.
At the same time, Trump has feted Putin, agreed to allow Russian diesel into global and US markets, and lifted oil sanctions on Moscow.
What does each side want from this meeting?
Russia
For President Putin, the meeting could provide a positive photo opportunity and a platform to project power while sidelining the Ukraine conflict, analysts say.
It will give him a “first among equals” position that he can display at home to show that he can influence Europe’s security architecture following the Ukraine war, Alexander Bratersky, a Moscow-based journalist and political analyst, told Al Jazeera.
China
Beijing has already been pushing for a resolution to the US war on Iran, which has impacted its own energy supplies.
China will also want to avoid being pulled into a nuclear treaty it had no part in establishing.
Last month, China’s Foreign Ministry said it would be “neither fair, reasonable nor realistic to ask China to join the so-called trilateral nuclear disarmament negotiations at this stage”.
US
Trump’s priority is to include both China and Russia in a new nuclear proliferation treaty, according to administration officials. “The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world. This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous,” Olivia Wales, a White House spokesperson, told reporters.
The president could also use the meeting to project his administration’s diplomatic influence, as Iran refuses to capitulate to US demands for ending the war and hand Washington a win.
Trump has also sought closer ties with Xi, Putin and North Korea’s Kim Jong Un, all seen as “strongmen”, and is likely to be perceived as influential in such circles, analysts say.
“I think it will be more performative – Donald Trump playing global statesman rather than peacemaker,” said Mabon.
Trump’s Republican Party’s crushing defeat in midterm elections last week could undermine his leverage, experts note, as a new Democrat-led Congress is likely to support Ukraine more staunchly.
Is this the start of a new Yalta?
Pyotr Tolstoy, chairman of the Russian parliament’s foreign affairs committee said it could lead to a “new Yalta”.
The 1945 conference in Yalta, in the then Soviet Union, saw USSR President Joseph Stalin, the US’s Franklin D Roosevelt, and the United Kingdom’s Winston Churchill divide Germany and establish the United Nations in what was seen as the template for a new world order.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, called the trilateral meeting now taking place between the leaders of the US, China and Russia as “extremely significant” but pointed out that any agreements reached at the meeting cannot be imposed on other nations.

Debiasing Law Enforcement Officers: Evidence from an Expressive Arts Intervention in India
Sofia Amaral, Girija Borker, Nishith Prakash, and María Micaela Sviatschi
NBER Working Paper No. 35986
November 2026
JEL No. O10, P0
ABSTRACT
Frontline state agents exercise substantial discretion over citizens’ access to public services, yet 
little is known about whether the attitudes and beliefs shaping this discretion can be changed among 
incumbent bureaucrats. Partnering with the Bihar Police - one of India’s largest states that operates 
under comparatively severe policing capacity constraints, we conduct a cluster randomized 
controlled trial across 417 police stations and roughly 2,500 active duty senior field police officers 
to evaluate a three-day expressive arts intervention, grounded in the Theatre of the Oppressed, 
designed to change police responses to gender-based violence (GBV). Approximately 7 months 
after baseline, treated officers exhibit more favorable attitudes toward GBV, greater empathy, and 
stronger legal knowledge. These changes translate into observed policing behavior: in standardized 
victim audits conducted one year later, officers in treated stations are 15 percentage points less 
likely to blame victims, dismiss fewer complaints, and provide more referrals, while administrative 
records show a 41 percent reduction in registration delays and, over a longer horizon, increased 
GBV reporting by citizens. Exploiting variation generated by officer transfers, we find suggestive 
evidence that these effects persist when treated officers relocate and diffuse to untreated officers 
working alongside treated colleagues. The effects also extend to the workplace: junior female 
officers working with treated senior officers report lower harassment and anxiety. These findings 
show that the attitudes shaping bureaucratic discretion are malleable and that changing how 
incumbent state agents exercise authority can improve both citizen-facing service delivery and the 
broader workplace environment.

1 Introduction
Improving the performance of frontline bureaucracies is central to building effective states (Besley
and Persson, 2009; Page and Pande, 2018). Existing research has emphasized the role of personnel
selection, incentives, and accountability in determining the quality of public services (e.g., Duflo
et al., 2012; Das et al., 2016; Finan et al., 2017). However, even when bureaucrats operate under the
same formal rules and incentives, frontline interactions often require substantial discretion, and
differences in officials’ attitudes, beliefs, and decision-making can shape the quality of services
citizens receive. Whether these attributes can be changed among incumbent state agents and
whether doing so improves their interactions with citizens, remains less well understood.
Law enforcement provides a particularly consequential setting in which to study this question.
Police officers routinely make high-stakes decisions about whether to take complaints seriously,
initiate formal procedures, and provide citizens with access to legal protections (Dube et al., 2025;
Amaral et al., 2025). Moreover, unlike many other public services, policing has no close private
substitute: the state retains a monopoly over the application of the law. Biases in the exercise of
police discretion can therefore restrict access to justice and weaken citizens’ willingness to engage
with the state.
These concerns are especially salient for gender-based violence (GBV), which is characterized
by stigma, fear of backlash, and forms of victimization that are frequently concealed from public
scrutiny (Murvartian et al., 2024). In this case, dismissive responses, victim-blaming, and proce-
dural barriers at police stations reduce reporting and perpetuate inequality in legal protection.1 In
response to these challenges, policymakers have turned to gender quotas which have increased
reporting crimes against women (Miller and Segal, 2019; Sukhtankar et al., 2022; Amaral et al.,
2021; Sviatschi and Trako, 2024; García-Hombrados et al., 2024; Asik et al., 2026; Bernhardt et al.,
2026). Yet policing remains a male-dominated and highly hierarchical profession, in which senior
officers exercise substantial discretion and tenure protections limit the scope for personnel real-
location.2 These institutional features raise a central question: can the attitudes and behavior of
1Despite high prevalence of GBV, women’s reporting rates remain extremely low, reflecting both social stigma and
institutional failure. Prior work shows that police officers’ attitudes toward GBV, such as beliefs about victim credi-
bility or whether sexual harassment merits police action, strongly shape officers’ behavior and affect crime incidence
(Amaral et al., 2025)
2In India, several states have adopted gender quotas in law enforcement. However, female recruitment remains
low, and quota thresholds are often not met (Tata Trusts, 2023). Qualitative evidence further suggests that female
officers face workplace harassment and hostile working conditions, potentially discouraging women from entering or
1
existing state agents be reshaped, and does doing so improve the services citizens receive?
This paper studies whether reshaping GBV attitudes and skills of senior police officers through
a novel expressive arts intervention can improve policing performance and the workplace envi-
ronment in the presence of entrenched gender bias. To study this question, we partner with the
Bihar Police in India, to implement a clustered randomized controlled trial covering 417 police
stations across twelve districts and roughly 2,500 active duty senior field police officers serving
42 million citizens. Bihar is the poorest state in India, and provides a particularly relevant con-
text: despite recent legislative improvements, gender violence remains highly prevalent, report-
ing rates are extremely low, and women remain underrepresented in decision-making roles within
police stations.3 Our intervention targets key decision-makers— Station House Officers, Inspec-
tors, Sub-Inspectors, and Assistant Sub-Inspectors—who shape both citizen-facing behavior and
internal workplace norms.4
Motivated by evidence that immersive and experiential learning can be more effective than
traditional instruction in shifting beliefs, norms, and decision-making in high-discretion settings
(Andries et al., 2024; Dube et al., 2025; Ashraf et al., 2024; Chaudhuri et al., 2025), we design a
novel expressive arts-based training tailored to address police biases towards GBV in India. The
intervention was informed by 18 months of qualitative fieldwork, including sustained observa-
tion in police stations and interviews with officers, GBV survivors, and civil society organizations.
This fieldwork highlighted two features of the police organization that shaped the program de-
sign: substantial discretion in officers’ responses to GBV and a highly hierarchical workplace in
which senior officers influence both case handling and norms of appropriate conduct.
The intervention therefore targets senior active duty field officers and combines perspective-
remaining in the police force. Moreover, most quotas apply to lower-ranking positions within police stations, limiting
women’s representation in decision-making roles. Indeed, Bernhardt et al. (2026) show experimentally that assigning
female constables to police stations increases GBV registration while, at the same time, male colleagues become more
likely to express biased beliefs about female complainants. This tension points to a distinct challenge: improving
representation may expand women’s access to the state without changing—and may in some cases reinforce—the
beliefs through which incumbent male officers exercise discretion.
3According to the Bihar Economic Survey 2025-26, Bihar’s per capita remains the lowest in India with a per capita
GDP at current prices of USD 925. Bihar’s GDP is comparable to those of other low-income countries such as Sierra
Leone, Uganda, or Gambia.
4Reforming the police has been a persistent challenge in Bihar. GBV remains widespread: 40 percent of women
aged 18–49 report having experienced spousal physical or sexual violence, yet only 2 percent of survivors seek help
from the police (NFHS-5, 2022, 2021). This gap persists despite the existence of formal legal protections against
domestic violence and a 35 percent gender quota in police recruitment (Tata Trusts, 2023). Moreover, women remain
underrepresented in decision-making roles within police stations, limiting their influence over frontline responses to
GBV.
2
taking, experiential learning, and collective reflection. It draws on Freirean conscientization (Freire,
1970) and Boal’s Theatre of the Oppressed (Boal, 2014), adapting these methods to policing and of-
ficers’ interactions with GBV survivors. Through role play and simulated police-station scenar-
ios, officers assume the perspectives of survivors and responding officers, confront competing
interpretations of the same situation, and collectively reflect on appropriate responses. Rather
than prescribing a single behavioral rule, the training exposes officers to context-rich scenarios in
which they must exercise judgment, with the aim of improving how they interpret situations and
use discretion. Guided reflection, peer feedback, and explicit commitments to station-level prac-
tice changes reinforce these experiences and create shared expectations about acceptable conduct
(Bicchieri, 2016).
We hypothesize that the intervention operates through two reinforcing channels. First, it
changes how officers interpret situations and exercise discretion by fostering perspective-taking
and empathy (individual attitudes channel). Second, because the training is delivered collectively
and publicly to senior officers from multiple stations, it creates shared experiences and expecta-
tions about appropriate conduct, potentially reshaping workplace norms and diffusing through
the police hierarchy (workplace channel). We use plausibly exogenous officer transfers to explore
the importance of these channels.5
Our analysis draws on a rich set of newly collected data that captures officer attitudes, be-
havior, and workplace dynamics using surveys, random victims’ audit data, and administrative
police records. We measure police officers’ mindsets, attitudes, and technical skills related to
GBV using detailed novel survey measures administered to senior male officers. We make use
of self-reported measures, along with vignettes, thus, taking into account possible measurement
concerns (Bursztyn et al., 2025). To measure real-world policing behavior, we implement a stan-
dardized victim audit in which trained decoys visit police stations to lodge complaints and sys-
tematically record officers’ responses, and we complement these measures with administrative
data on crime registration and handling drawn from approximately 500,000 official police records.
To assess changes in the workplace environment and potential spillovers, we conducted confiden-
tial surveys of junior female constables at treated and control police stations. These officers were
5Separating these channels experimentally would require independently varying the individual perspective-
taking component and the collective exposure of officers within stations. Such a factorial design was not feasible
because the training was designed and delivered as a single integrated program rather than as separable modules. We
therefore rely on plausibly exogenous officer transfers to distinguish patterns consistent with persistent individual-
level change from those consistent with workplace norm diffusion.
3
not targeted by the intervention, allowing us to measure whether the intervention affected their
experiences of harassment, anxiety, and perceptions of senior officers. In addition, we use data on
officer transfers to examine the mechanisms underlying the intervention’s effects and the extent
to which those effects spillover to untreated officers. Together, these data allow us to link changes
in officer attitudes to downstream changes in workplace culture and service delivery.
We find that immersive expressive-arts training significantly improves police attitudes and
thus, performance, workplace environment, and interactions with survivors of GBV. In particular,
we find that treated senior officers exhibit greater empathy, stronger beliefs in the credibility of
survivors’ complaints, and greater legal and procedural knowledge. Approximately one year
after the intervention, standardized victim audits show that these changes are accompanied by
substantial improvements in real-world police behavior: officers are less likely to dismiss cases or
blame victims and more likely to provide appropriate guidance and referrals.
Consistent with these behavioral changes, administrative data show that officers in treated
police stations register GBV cases more quickly following reported incidents, indicating improved
responsiveness in formalizing complaints. We also find that treated officers devote more time to
investigating and following up on GBV cases. Furthermore, after one year, we observe an increase
in the overall volume of GBV First Information Reports (FIRs). Importantly, this increase emerges
only after earlier improvements in officer attitudes, behavior, and responsiveness, a sequence
consistent with improved service delivery increasing victims’ willingness to seek help and engage
with the justice system.
We also provide suggestive evidence on the mechanisms underlying these effects. We exploit
officer transfers across police stations, which are frequent in the Indian bureaucracy (Iyer and
Mani, 2012), to examine whether the effects persist with treated officers and diffuse to untreated
colleagues.6 Treated officers who move to control stations retain improvements in GBV attitudes,
consistent with a persistent individual-level change that survives a change in workplace envi-
ronment. At the same time, untreated officers who move into treated stations exhibit sizable
improvements, consistent with exposure to treated peers and station-level norm diffusion. Taken
together, these patterns suggest that the intervention operates through a combination of durable
6Transfers are not randomly assigned. They are common in the Indian bureaucracy and often occur for adminis-
trative reasons, but they may also reflect political considerations, disciplinary actions, officer requests, or responses
to major incidents. We therefore interpret the transfer analysis as suggestive evidence on persistence and diffusion
rather than as a source of exogenous variation.
4
individual change and changes in workplace norms.
The effects also extend beyond directly treated officers to the broader workplace environment.
Eight months after the training, junior female officers stationed with treated senior officers report
significantly lower levels of workplace harassment and anxiety, suggesting that changes in senior
officers’ behavior affect not only their interactions with GBV survivors but also how senior officers
exercise authority within the police organization.
Several pieces of evidence make alternative explanations based on changes in formal incen-
tives, sample composition, social desirability, or short-run monitoring less likely. First, the in-
tervention did not alter officers’ formal responsibilities, compensation, promotion prospects, or
enforcement intensity, making explanations based on changes in formal incentives less likely.
Second, results are robust to controlling for the share of female officers, and social desirability
measures.7 The fact that we also detect changes in performance using audit data, and among
non-treated officers (females and non-treated transferred officers) further reassures that results
are not driven by these measurement concerns. Third, we also find that treatment effects do
not vary with officers’ rank or hierarchical position, which would be expected if changes were
primarily driven by senior officers rewarding visible compliance. Moreover, key outcomes are
measured well after the training—approximately one year later in the standardized victim audits
and over an even longer horizon in the administrative records. The audits capture behavior in
settings where officers were unaware of being evaluated, while the administrative records are
generated independently of the research team, reducing concerns about short-run signaling or
experimenter demand effects. Together, these patterns support an interpretation in which the in-
tervention operates through shifts in officer attitudes and decision-making rather than through
mechanical channels.
This paper contributes to the literature on public service delivery (e.g., Finan et al., 2017; Ra-
sul and Rogger, 2018) and frontline workers (Maynard-Moody and Musheno, 2003) by providing
causal evidence that an intervention targeting attitudes, and decision-making among state agents
can improve performance in a high-discretion institutional setting. Prior work on policing shows
how officers’ decision making is affected by their attitudes and prevalent social norms (Amaral
et al., 2025), but there is limited evidence on whether interventions can generate persistent be-
7As we will explain, our novel measures include a mix of direct-questioning and vignettes – tools designed to
mitigate concerns over desirability bias (Bursztyn et al., 2025).
5
havioral change among frontline bureaucrats or service providers – key agents in GBV response.
We show that an immersive, experiential training targeting senior police officers significantly im-
proves both attitudes and real-world behavior toward victims of GBV. Thereby establishing a
direct link between bias reduction and service quality in a core state function. Unlike reforms that
rely on changing personnel composition or creating parallel institutions, our intervention oper-
ates within the existing hierarchy, targeting decision-makers who shape both case outcomes and
workplace norms. The results suggest that attitudes, norms and institutional culture are integral
components of public sector performance. More broadly, by targeting senior officers within hi-
erarchical police stations, we complement recent work on the role of public-sector managers in
shaping the performance of government agencies (Fenizia, 2022). Our findings suggest that man-
agers may influence not only organizational performance and worker effort, but also workplace
norms, discretionary behavior, and the treatment of vulnerable citizens.
Second, we contribute to the experimental literature on police training (Dube et al., 2025; Bern-
hardt et al., 2026; Harris et al., 2022; Banerjee et al., 2021; Canales et al., 2025). Closely related, Dube
et al. (2025) show that experiential training can induce a “cognitive pause” in high-stress policing
environments and reduce use of force. We build on this work by studying a different source of
discretionary failure: gender bias in officers’ interactions with survivors of GBV. We show that
experiential training can generate persistent changes in attitudes and service quality. We further
combine survey measures with standardized victim audits and administrative records, allowing
us to trace effects from individual attitudes to real-world police behavior as well as quantifying
spillover effects on untreated officers.
Finally, we contribute to the literature on gender norms, perspective-taking, and experien-
tial learning (e.g., Dhar et al., 2022; Sharma, 2024; Chaudhuri et al., 2025; Banerjee et al., 2019;
Andries et al., 2024; Ashraf et al., 2024). This literature shows that narratives, curricula, and par-
ticipatory interventions can shift attitudes. Most closely related, Chaudhuri et al. (2025) study
Jana Sanskriti’s community-based participatory theater in West Bengal and find changes in the
acceptability of domestic violence and women’s voice. We bring these insights into a markedly
different institutional setting: a hierarchical state bureaucracy in which participants themselves
exercise substantial authority over citizens. Rather than seeking to change norms among citizens,
our intervention seeks to change how incumbent state agents interpret situations and exercise
discretion. Our setting allows us to study whether experiential methods designed to challenge
deeply rooted social norms can alter the behavior of state agents, whether these changes persist,


[…]

. These
patterns are consistent with a workplace diffusion channel: officers who were not directly treated
nonetheless improve when exposed to treated peers, potentially through learning, imitation, or
shifts in perceived expectations within stations.
Taken together, the transfer-based heterogeneity analysis suggests that the intervention oper-
ates through a combination of persistent individual-level changes and station-level norm diffu-
sion. To further examine the role of workplace environment, we next estimate spillover effects on
junior women constables who were not trained.

6.4.2 Organizational Spillovers and Workplace Culture
If the intervention altered station-level norms or supervisory practices, its effects may extend
beyond treated officers to colleagues who did not participate in the intervention. We examine this

Whether training programs can generate broader changes in organizational culture remains far
from established, particularly in public-sector settings.18 Table 6 shows a test of whether the

We find that eight months after the intervention, female officers in treated stations report sig-
nificantly improved workplace environments, with the overall workplace anxiety index declining

that improved organizational climate for women, consistent with a mechanism in which training

of the intervention points to a station-level channel operating through supervisory practices and

This spillover is economically consequential. Because workplace harassment and violence are
themselves drivers of women leaving their jobs (Adams-Prassl et al., 2024) and of the occupational
segregation and pay gaps that follow (Folke and Rickne, 2022). A reduction in anxiety and harass-
ment among junior women is not merely a marker of improved culture but a plausible channel for
retaining women in a heavily male-dominated institution, fostering a more gender-equal police
force both in the immediate term but also in terms of the pipeline of officers.
7 Cost and Benchmarking
The training curriculum and its delivery were funded by the Fund for Innovation in Develop-
ment (FID), separately from the accompanying research and evaluation activities (officer surveys,
standardized victim audits, and administrative data collection), which were funded through the
J-PAL Crime and Violence Initiative and the J-PAL Gender Initiative.20 The cost of delivering the
intervention was EUR 136,560 (USD 151,600), approximately USD 108 per officer trained and USD
699 per treated station. The 217 treated stations serve an estimated 21.8 million residents; spread
across that population, the one-time delivery cost is under one US cent per resident. The training
is a one-time investment in officers, but its potential benefits extend to the much larger population
these officers serve.
At USD 108 per officer and an estimated effect of 0.082 standard deviations on the GBV at-
titudes index, the implied cost is approximately USD 1,320 per standard deviation of attitude
change. This is a cost-effectiveness metric rather than a welfare metric: it relates program cost di-
rectly to measured impact without requiring a monetary valuation of changes in GBV outcomes.
If these effects persist, this one-time cost is more appropriately expressed on an annualized basis:
USD 108 per officer if the effects last only one year, falling to as little as USD 22 per officer per
year if they persist for five. Appendix E reports these calculations under alternative persistence
assumptions.
To our knowledge, no published study reports both the cost and the impact of a police-focused
psychological well-being. We find no detectable effects on either depression (PHQ-9) or anxiety (GAD-7), suggesting
that improvements in GBV-related attitudes and behavior were not accompanied by deterioration in these dimensions
of officers’ mental health.
20See Appendix E for the full cost breakdown by component and category, cost shares, and the underlying calcula-
tions.
34
gender-based-violence training program specifically: the closest police intervention, the Women’s
Help Desk reform evaluated by Sukhtankar et al. (2022), is a bundled reform rather than a stand-
alone training and does not report costs on a comparable basis. This limits the scope for bench-
marking on a common cost basis. Our intervention produces effects at three levels: officers’ atti-
tudes and technical skills, their case-handling behavior in standardized audits, and administrative
case registration. No single external study speaks to all three, so we benchmark each against the
closest available evidence (Appendix E reports the full comparison).
On cost, the program is inexpensive in absolute terms, approximately USD 108 per officer
for a three-day training with follow-up and monitoring. The closest comparator that is itself a
behavioral training for serving police and reports both cost and field impact, the 16-hour Sit-D
program in Chicago, which cut uses of force and discretionary arrests by about 23 percent, cost
USD 807 to 864 per officer trained (Dube et al., 2025); we do not read the gap as a like-for-like
efficiency comparison, since cross-country training costs are dominated by local wage levels. On
attitudes, the training’s effect on officers’ GBV attitudes was on the order of half the standardized
effect of a 2.5-year, 28-session gender-attitudes curriculum for adolescents in India, a population
generally taken to be more malleable and reached over far more contact time (Dhar et al., 2022);
because the two indices measure different attitudes, this comparison is only approximate. On the
behavioral and administrative outcomes of most direct policy relevance, the closest comparator
is again Sukhtankar et al. (2022), which raised the number of women’s cases formally registered.
Our training moved that same registration margin, raising GBV reporting over the longer run,
and additionally reduced the delay between a reported incident and its registration by 41 percent,
a margin that study did not examine.
Beyond cost, the intervention’s significance lies in where its measured effects sit in the broader
chain from policing to women’s welfare. The attitudes, case-handling, and registration outcomes
we document are the proximate margins through which frontline policing shapes whether women
seek and obtain redress. More effective redress can, in turn, alter women’s perceived risks from
participating in public life and reduce the need for costly avoidance responses. A companion
police experiment in Hyderabad makes this downstream link concrete: where uniformed patrols
reduced severe public-space sexual harassment, women became roughly 30 percent less likely
to move elsewhere in response to it, easing constraints on physical mobility that are linked to
women’s schooling (Borker, ming) and labor force participation. Such changes can affect la-
bor supply on both the extensive margin—whether women work at all—and the intensive mar-
35
gin—where, when, and how much they work. In Hyderabad, police visibility and officers’ at-
titudes toward harassment were central to the effect (Amaral et al., 2025), the same attitudinal
margin targeted by our intervention. A training that improves these attitudes and the quality of
redress at modest cost may therefore have consequences that extend beyond police performance
to women’s willingness to take risks, participate in public spaces, and pursue economic opportu-
nities, even where we do not attach a dollar value to these downstream benefits.
8 Conclusion
Public institutions frequently fail citizens not only because of limited resources or weak incentives,
but also because of the beliefs and biases of the frontline agents who deliver the state’s services.
Policing makes this especially consequential. Officers exercise substantial discretion over which
complaints are registered, how survivors are treated, and whether the law is applied consistently.
Unlike most public services, policing has no private substitute. When this discretion is shaped by
entrenched gender norms, access to justice becomes unequal precisely for those who depend on
the state most.
This paper asks whether the performance of an existing, hierarchical, and male-dominated
police force can be improved by reshaping the attitudes and skills of the officers who already staff
it. Partnering with the Government of Bihar, we implemented a clustered randomized evaluation
of a three-day expressive arts curriculum, grounded in the Theatre of the Oppressed, delivered
to senior officers in 417 police stations. Approximately 7 months after the baseline, treated of-
ficers exhibit significant improvements in attitudes toward GBV, higher empathy, and stronger
legal and procedural knowledge. These gains translate into real-world behavior. Standardized
victim audits conducted roughly one year later show that treated officers are less likely to dismiss
complaints or blame survivors and more likely to provide appropriate guidance and referrals,
and administrative records show that stations register cases substantially more quickly after an
incident occurs. Over a longer horizon, reports of GBV rise in treated stations, consistent with
improved police responsiveness increasing survivors’ willingness to seek help.
Beyond documenting that bias among state agents is malleable, the paper provides evidence
on how change emerges and why it persists. Exploiting plausibly exogenous officer transfers, we
show that treated officers continue to improve after moving to stations where no peer was trained,
36
while untreated officers improve after moving into treated stations. Together with lower reported
harassment and anxiety among junior female constables, who were never targeted by the inter-
vention, these patterns point to two reinforcing channels: durable individual-level change in how
officers interpret situations and exercise discretion, and the diffusion of new norms through the
station hierarchy. The sequence of effects is itself informative. Improvements in officer attitudes,
conduct, and responsiveness appear first, while increases in citizen reporting emerge only with a
lag, consistent with better service delivery gradually rebuilding trust rather than with mechanical
compliance or short-run experimenter demand.
These findings speak to a central question in the study of state capacity. Whereas many re-
forms seek to improve service delivery by changing who provides it, through female recruitment,
gender quotas, specialized courts, or dedicated women’s police stations, we show that the behav-
ior of the officers already in place can be reshaped from within. This distinction matters in set-
tings where governments struggle to recruit and retain women despite formal quotas, and where
tenure protections limit personnel reallocation. By targeting senior officers who shape both case
outcomes and workplace norms, the intervention operates on the decision-makers whose discre-
tion is most consequential for survivors.
More broadly, our results suggest that improving governance may require addressing the so-
cial and organizational foundations of bureaucratic behavior. Citizens do not experience the state
in the abstract; they experience it through a single interaction with a frontline official, and the
quality of that interaction can determine whether the law reaches them at all. Interventions that
cultivate perspective-taking and reshape workplace norms can change how those interactions
unfold, generating durable improvements in the treatment of vulnerable citizens and offering a
scalable path to strengthening state capacity in high-discretion institutional settings.
37

Commerce Department under pressure for delaying export controls on Nvidia chips
The U.S. Commerce Department is under scrutiny for clearing Chinese companies to handle Nvidia chips, despite national security concerns from cabinet officials and U.S. intelligence agencies.
ROB SCHMITZ, HOST:
Pressure is growing on the Commerce Department and its Secretary Howard Lutnick over why Nvidia's chips have been allowed to be exported to China, despite national security concerns from cabinet officials and intelligence agencies.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
SCOTT BESSENT: They were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months, but commerce has the pin. Commerce BIS has the pin, and you will have to ask them about their internal processes.
SCHMITZ: That is Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent accusing Lutnick's department of not putting Megaspeed, a Singapore-based firm with suspected Chinese intelligence ties, on the federal trade restriction list. Liza Tobin is former China director for the National Security Council in the first Trump and Biden administrations. She's here with us now to discuss this. Welcome.
LIZA TOBIN: Thanks for having me, Rob.
SCHMITZ: So you're watching this situation unfold very closely. Tell me your reaction to these accusations against Secretary Lutnick.
TOBIN: Commerce has the pen. Commerce is the agency that has been given the statutory authority by the Congress to regulate the export of these AI chips. They're the ones that write the rules. They also have a law enforcement role. Right now, the whole cover has been blown off this scandal, and Lutnick is there at the center, and it's clear that he just didn't do his job in enforcing those rules.
SCHMITZ: Why do you think that is?
TOBIN: So that is the trillion-dollar question. I think we're going to find out a lot more as Congress starts to dig into this. I think we're going to learn a lot more about, was Howard Lutnick benefiting from this regulatory capture? You know, he...
SCHMITZ: Well, I mean, we do know that Cantor Fitzgerald, a firm run by Lutnick's sons Brandon and Kyle, helps place companies that run data centers in Asia, and their firm has a financial interest in looser chip restrictions that Lutnick himself was in charge of implementing. That seems like a conflict of interest, no?
TOBIN: It absolutely looks like a conflict of interest. And what's clear is that the rest of the president's advisors - Scott Bessent, the tech advisor Michael Kratsios, the director of national intelligence Jay Clayton, Marco Rubio, and others - were all on one side of this issue, advising the president - Mr. President, we've got to close these loopholes and prevent China from accessing our compute. Remember, the president had changed the policy to say, we can sell the previous generation of Nvidia chips, the so-called H 200...
SCHMITZ: The less powerful chips.
TOBIN: That's right. But the president said we are not going to sell the Blackwell chips, at the time the most advanced. Now we know that a whole lot of these Blackwell chips have either been smuggled or they're being accessed by Chinese AI developers overseas in data centers in Malaysia. So you're absolutely right to point to Cantor's interest in seeing that data center trade continue to grow. He disobeyed the president. The president told him to address this three times, so when is that going to happen?
SCHMITZ: I want to - and I want to ask you about that. I mean, this is the Trump administration. The buck stops with President Trump. How much should we be looking at whether President Trump allowed this to happen?
TOBIN: I was advising President Trump when he made the difficult decision to initially put export controls on ships going to Huawei, this giant Chinese telecom. It was a difficult decision because no one knew what the implications would be. It was kind of the first time doing such a dramatic policy move, but he made that decision himself. So I don't think the president is sort of deeply wedded to one view or the other, but he has been persuaded that it's now a good idea to close these loopholes. He told Lutnick to do that, and he was dragging his feet. And so I think the Congress is going to be, you know, calling him in to testify.
SCHMITZ: OK, so you seem to be focused here on Howard Lutnick and his culpability in all of this. What do we know about the relationship between Jensen Huang, the former CEO now of Invidia, and Secretary Lutnick?
TOBIN: We know the president likes very wealthy and powerful men and geniuses like Jensen Huang. And so he sort of got his ticket into the White House. Jensen was in the cool kids club. Everybody wanted to be in the same room as Jensen Huang. In some ways, he was more powerful than the cabinet secretaries himself. I thought of Jensen Huang as almost, like, the chief technology officer of the United States. He was in explaining AI, explaining chips. It was Jensen Huang's view of the world, telling the president, hey, it's a good idea to sell American technology. These are just kind of old, outdated chips. It's a good idea to sell these chips to China and keep China addicted to our tech stack.
SCHMITZ: It's important to point out here that these chips are not just being used for AI chatbots. They have military applications.
TOBIN: China has a long track record of using American technology to advance its own military ambitions. The thing that we have to remember is that China is really good at making a lot of kinds of technology, but they still are nowhere close to being able to produce chips anywhere close to the level of Nvidia's most advanced chips. Anyone in China that wants to be doing cutting-edge AI really wants these chips. And what are they going to use them for? Better missile guidance, its hypersonic missiles, its undersea warfare. It's only a matter of time before China develops its own cyber-capable models that can launch massive disruptive AI-disabled attacks. And by giving them access to the best American chips, it allows them to get there faster. The race to lead in AI is one that is winnable for the United States, but only if we have a government that's taking it seriously and actually has a strategy. I do think that the new Congress coming in is going to be hyperfocused on this issue. They're going to be calling all these folks in to testify, and they're going to put a lot of pressure on them to close the loopholes.
SCHMITZ: That is Liza Tobin, former China director for the National Security Council. Thank you.
TOBIN: Thanks for having me, Rob.
(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)
SCHMITZ: We reached out to the White House and the Commerce Department for a response to Liza Tobin's comments. A spokesperson for the Commerce Department sent us this statement. Quote, "the secretary has fully complied with the terms of his ethics agreement, including all divestiture and recusal requirements, and will continue to do so. He has divested all financial interests in Cantor Fitzgerald, Newmark, and BGC."
